sources.title: Kamal-ol-molk (Q1659496), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-01): label 'Kamal-ol-molk', description 'Iranian artist (1847-1940)', preferred birth value 1848-09-29 (other values 1847 and 1848 are present, one marked deprecated), death 1940-08-18, citizen of Iran, no Korean label. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Kamal-al-Molk, Mohammad Ghaffari', part i 'Life' (Encyclopaedia Iranica Foundation, vol. XV, fasc. 4, 2010; read in full, about 5,000 words). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: the entry's lead calls him a widely acclaimed Iranian painter of the European academic style during the late Qajar and early Pahlavi periods; it covers the Dar al-Fonun training, the court career from about 1880, the Hall of Mirrors painting, the 1898 journey to Europe, the departure from court and the 1911 founding of the Academy of Fine Arts, the 1920s conflicts with education ministers and his 1927 resignation, and it explicitly separates the documented record from a later romantic and political myth about him. Passages on his marriages, family, temper, love affair, eye injury and Constitutional-era politics were read and are not scored.

Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Kamal-al-Molk, Mohammad Ghaffari', part ii 'Style' (read in full, about 4,500 words). Scholarly account of his training in academic painting, the court years and his plein-air work, the study of the old masters in Florence and Paris, the Academy and its curriculum, his statement about his models (Raphael and Rembrandt), and a survey of critical opinion: admiring students (Ashtiani, Shaykh), who praise his accuracy and say he revolutionised Persian painting but note weakness in composition, and modernist critics (Aghdashlou, Vaziri-Moqaddam), who say he merely copied nature and discouraged an authentic Persian modern art. CRITICAL / COUNTER-VOICE source.

Layla S. Diba, 'Muhammad Ghaffari: The Persian Painter of Modern Life', Iranian Studies 45(5), 2012, pp. 645-659 (Cambridge Core page; only the abstract was readable, the article itself is behind a paywall and was not opened). Scholarly abstract: leading court painter of the late Qajar period, recognised early as the leading exponent of academic painting, whose art by the constitutional period had moved to a style representing contemporary Persian life, with attention to his training, photography, the European journey and parallels with the Ottoman painter Osman Hamdi.

Rute Ferreira, 'Painting of the Week: Kamal-ol-Molk and the Perfection of the Mirror Hall', DailyArt Magazine, 17 June 2018 (read in full, about 600 words; a popular art magazine). Describes the Hall of Mirrors painting (1885-1890, Golestan Palace) as his best-known work, which took five years, its detail and verisimilitude and play of light and shadow, and his later study of classical artists in Europe. Popular source: used for the Hall of Mirrors description only.

'Kamal-ol-Molk', Iran Chamber Society, Iranian Visual Arts (read in full, about 1,500 words; an Iranian cultural-society website with an admiring, national-pride tone and no named author). Used only for facts that Encyclopaedia Iranica also states: the Dar al-Fonun training, the European study and copying of old masters, the art school with its carpet-weaving and wood-work classes, and the allotment of part of his salary to poor students. Its account of the later years as an exile for love of freedom is the political myth that Encyclopaedia Iranica rejects, and it is not used.

Sharafat (Sherafat), no. 60, Ramadan 1319 AH (about December 1901 to January 1902), p. 1: portrait lithograph of Kamal-ol-Molk signed by Mehdi Mossavar al-Molk, captioned 'Jenab-e Jalalatma'ab Kamal-ol-Molk, naqqashbashi-ye makhsus-e hozur-e homayun'. Digitised by the Universitats- und Landesbibliothek Bonn (Translatio project), record 7070386, marked Public Domain Mark 1.0 in the library's METS metadata. Used for the portrait only, not for any trait row.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_kamal_iranica_life, src_kamal_iranica_style, src_kamal_iranchamber, src_kamal_dailyart, src_kamal_diba | 1860s-1901 | scholarly encyclopedia + popular sources + scholarly abstract] After about eight years at Dar al-Fonun he was court painter by about 1880; in 1898, given the choice of a reward by the new Shah, he asked to go to Europe to improve his technical mastery and stayed about three years in Florence and Paris, making copies of Rembrandt's Saint Matthew and Titian's Entombment and, according to Iranica, advancing his knowledge of perspective, which he had first worked out by his own practice; Iran Chamber and DailyArt say he studied classical artists. The core fact (a study trip requested as his reward and aimed at technique) is documented in the scholarly entry and echoed by popular sources; the claim that his copies were indistinguishable from the originals appears only in the popular source and is not used. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (lead review, before eligibility): mastery_orientation lowered from 76 / 0.66 to 72 / 0.58 because mastery is read mostly from his finished paintings and an encyclopedia; the habits of study are documented thinly and partly through his own memoir.

detail_orientation.rationale: [src_kamal_iranica_style, src_kamal_iranica_life, src_kamal_dailyart | 1880-1900 | scholarly encyclopedia + critics + popular press] Iranica says his palace and landscape views surpassed his contemporaries in almost photographic naturalism and attention to detail, that the Hall of Mirrors occupied him for almost five years, and that he painted en plein air; his student Ashtiani praises his accuracy of design and painstaking attention to detail, and the modernist critic Vaziri-Moqaddam, who is hostile to him, makes the same observation in negative form (he 'photographed nature'); DailyArt notes the verisimilitude of each object in the Hall of Mirrors. Praise and criticism converge on exactness, which supports the trait, but the exactness is read from the finished works and critics' descriptions rather than from reports of his working habits. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (lead review, before eligibility): detail_orientation lowered from 78 / 0.62 to 72 / 0.54 because the claim comes from stylistic assessments of the paintings, not from documented working method.

autonomy_need.rationale: [src_kamal_iranica_life, src_kamal_iranica_style | 1898-1927 | scholarly encyclopedia] Iranica reports that he requested the European study leave partly to find a way out of court life and later admitted his relations with the new sovereign were uneasy; that under Mozaffar al-Din Shah he evaded unwelcome demands and left Tehran for Baghdad and Karbala for about two years; that he declined a well-paid portrait commission from the next Shah despite financial difficulty; and that in the 1920s he regarded himself as above the education ministry's new regulations and resigned in 1927. He also said he learned painting from no one but himself, although his teacher was an academy graduate. The independence is documented across decades, but the main accounts of the earlier episodes come from his own memoir and from friends' recollections, and Iranica itself warns that later writers inflated his resistance into a political legend, which is not scored here. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): reviewed as a top-risk row; lowered from 72 / 0.60 to 68 / 0.52 because the key episodes rest on his own memoir and friends' recollections rather than independent records.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_kamal_iranica_life, src_kamal_iranica_style, src_kamal_iranchamber | 1911-1927 | scholarly encyclopedia + society website] Iranica says he had long aspired to create a painting school, that the Academy of Fine Arts opened in 1911 with a state site and budget and he remained its director into the 1920s, that its alumni formed a school of followers and its curriculum added carpet weaving and lithography, and that he lived at the school, had lunch with the students and paid stipends to needy students from his own salary (via a friend's account), a detail also given by the Iran Chamber page. The institution-building and teaching are well documented; the stipend and generosity details come from admiring friends' accounts.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_kamal_iranica_style, src_kamal_iranica_life, src_kamal_diba | 1885-1911 | scholarly encyclopedia + scholarly abstract] Iranica says his move from the hybrid Euro-Persian style to a purely European naturalism was praised by students as revolutionising Persian painting but criticised by modernist critics for draining Persian painting of its anti-naturalistic qualities and for emulating nature; it also notes that after his time in Iraq his subjects shifted to urban scenes and the everyday life of ordinary people, a major evolution in Persian painting's imagery, and Diba's abstract says his style moved toward a representation of contemporary Persian life. Because the assessments are sharply divided and he himself said he modelled himself on Raphael and Rembrandt, the originality is scored only mildly.

portrait.source: Portrait lithograph of Kamal-ol-Molk, signed by Mehdi Mossavar al-Molk, printed as the full-page frontispiece of the Tehran periodical Sharafat (Sherafat) no. 60, Ramadan 1319 AH (about December 1901 to January 1902), with the printed caption naming 'Kamal-ol-Molk, naqqashbashi (chief painter) to His Majesty's presence'; Encyclopaedia Iranica independently records that Sharafat no. 60 (1902) carried his portrait drawn by Mossavar al-Molk. A depiction made in his lifetime by another artist, not a documented sitting or photograph, so recorded as a historical depiction. Rights basis: the holder of the digitised periodical, the Universitats- und Landesbibliothek Bonn (record 7070386, Translatio project), states in its METS metadata that the work is under Public Domain Mark 1.0; independent of that, the print was published in Tehran in 1902, i.e. before 1931, so it is in the public domain in the United States by age (as far as I could establish Iran was not a Berne or UCC partner, so no URAA restoration is expected), and nothing in the record claims a conflicting copyright. Caveats: the Commons file (File:Sharafat, Issue 60, p. 01.png, 4096 x 5120 pixels, originally a scan of a bound volume that may be a later reprint of the 1900s original) carries a PD-Iran tag and the library's PD mark; I could not open the library's live viewer (it served a browser-verification page), so the rights statement was read from the library's OAI-PMH METS record instead; the creator Mossavar al-Molk's death date was not established. The image used here is a crop of the framed portrait and its caption from that page (the surrounding book margins and the facing page removed), downscaled from a 2100 x 2880 crop to 875 x 1200 pixels, never upscaled.
portrait.license: Public domain (published 1902; Public Domain Mark 1.0 by the digitising library)

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: PLAUSIBLE (lead-robust) (lead) / CONFIRMED VIA A REPLACEMENT, after the lead's self-portrait path failed on item-level facts: the Malek National Museum records for the 1315 and 1336 AH self-portraits say the artist is only 'probably' Kamal-ol-Molk and the museum site reserves all rights (print reproduction only with prior permission); the Doha 'MIA.2014.552.1' file is contradicted by a sister Commons file placing the same painting at Sa'dabad Palace, so its holder is uncertain; the 1922 Parliament-museum self-portrait comes from ical.ir, which was blocked (403) so its terms could not be read; the Smithsonian (Freer-Sackler) Sevruguin studio photograph is rejected because the collection finding aid (FSA A.04) says permission to publish or reproduce must be secured from the repository, whatever Commons says. Replacement: a lifetime portrait lithograph in the 1902 periodical Sharafat no. 60, digitised by the University Library Bonn with a Public Domain Mark, which Iranica independently dates and attributes. PREFLIGHT: QID VERIFIED LIVE (2026-11-01) Q1659496 label 'Kamal-ol-molk', description 'Iranian artist (1847-1940)'; birth year 1848 is the Wikidata preferred value (Iranica discusses 1848 as the widely accepted date and argues for about 1859, other sources say 1847), death 1940-08-18; no production (prod62.txt) or candidate slug/QID collision. REGION west_asia (Iran; precedents hafez, ferdowsi, abbas-kiarostami). ERA 19th_century (court career and best-known works 1880-1900; academy 1911-1927). ZERO POLITICS: his sympathy for the Constitutional Revolution, Freemasonry membership, the conflict with Reza Khan and the 'exile' story are not scored; the refusal of a royal portrait commission and the resignation from the ministry are used only as evidence about working autonomy and are not scored as political acts. VOCABULARY: occupations painter, teacher; fields art, education; tags mentor, craft_focused; archetype creative_creator; impact domains artistic, cultural, educational (all present in en.ts and ko.ts). KOREAN NAME: no Korean Wikipedia or Wikidata label exists; '카말올몰크' is a recorded transliteration of Kamal-ol-molk. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Kamal-al-Molk, Mohammad Ghaffari' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/kamal-al-molk-mohammad-gaffari/), parts i and ii, read in full. READ: Iranica life and style; DailyArt Magazine; Iran Chamber Society; Tehran Times notice on the Malek Museum exhibition (read, not cited: it repeats the exile story that Iranica rejects); Cambridge abstract of Diba 2012 (abstract only). PERSPECTIVES: scholarly encyclopedia, admiring students, modernist critics (inside Iranica), popular art press, cultural-society website, scholarly abstract. COUNTER-VOICES: modernist critics Aghdashlou and Vaziri-Moqaddam (read through Iranica) on naturalism and its effect on Persian art; Iranica's own correction of the heroic myth. NOT OPENED: Diba's full article (paywalled), the primary memoir and letters (Kamal-al-Molk's own writings, Ghani's Yadnama, Foroughi) known only through Iranica, Britannica (403), the Alzahra Hall-of-Mirrors article (connection failed), the Majlis museum site (403). SELF-REPORT SEPARATION: his own memoir statements (about leaving court, learning painting by himself, his models) reach us through Iranica and are treated as self-report; no row rests on them alone. EXCLUSIONS (hard rule): marriages, separation from family, the love affair, temper, eye injury, bereavement and all health matters are not used and no trait is inferred from them. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): top-risk rows reviewed: autonomy_need (72/0.60 lowered to 68/0.52), detail_orientation (kept: praise and hostile criticism converge on exactness), impact_motivation (kept at 64/0.52: school-building is documented, stipend details are friends' accounts).
